newsitem.title: SWEDEN: S-E-Banken 9 mo profit soars, loan losses slump.
newsitem.headline: S-E-Banken 9 mo profit soars, loan losses slump.

text.p: Swedish commercial bank S-E-Banken on Tuesday reported more than double earnings in the first nine months of 1996 but said personnel costs had risen by 12 percent despite lower staff numbers.
The boost in operating profits was mainly due to a slump in loan losses to 1.23 billion crowns ($186.4 million) from 3.61 billion crowns in the same 1995 period.
S-E-Banken 9 mo profit soars, loan losses=2
Operating profits themselves -- often referred to as profit after credit losses -- rose to 4.42 billion crowns ($670.1 million) compared with 2.06 billion for the first three quarters of last year.
Top line earnings received a sharp boost as interest costs fell seven percent to 16.89 billion crowns, whilst interest income was down just three percent to 22.10 billion.

"This increase is mainly explained by falling market rates, which led to an improved yield on the bank's bond portfolios and to lower costs of financing the bank's problem assets, mainly Diligentia," S-E-Banken said in a statement.

Property unit Diligentia was spun off to shareholders earlier this year in a move that marked an end to the bank's unwilling involvement in the real estate market following the property crash in Sweden in the early 1990s.
Commission on investment banking operations was also strongly ahead, with commission income minus costs contributing 3.43 billion crowns to consolidated earnings.
The only blemish on an otherwise strong interim report was a 12 percent rise in staff costs to 3.93 billion crowns, despite a fall in total personnel numbers.
With interest margins declining and credit losses down at manageable levels, costs in the Swedish banking system have come under closer scrutiny.
"Staff costs increased...despite a reduction of close to 200 in the number of positions compared with the first three quarters of 1995," the bank said.
"A considerable part of the increase was due to allocations to the bank's profit-sharing system."
S-E-Banken's nine month report was continued proof that the bank has returned to financial health.
Lending losses now correspond to just 0.65 percent of the total loan portfolio, whilst doubtful claims declined 42 percent to a net of 4.78 billion crowns.
The disposal of Dilligentia also meant a fall in the volume of pledges taken over to 2.01 billion crowns from a staggering 15.28 billion in the same 1995 period.
The share market gave the report a positive reception, and S-E-Banken stock rose one crown to 56.50 on an otherwise soft market.
-- Trevor Datson, Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700 1006 ($ = 6.596 Swedish Crowns)
